newsitem.title: Australia: British yachtsman may need hospital care.
newsitem.headline: British yachtsman may need hospital care.

text.p: Rescued British yachtsman Tony Bullimore appeared on Saturday to be in worse condition than first thought, with the Australian government saying he may need to be treated in hospital when the rescue ship docks.
"The captain of HMAS Adelaide reports Mr Bullimore may require hospitalisation when he arrives on Monday," Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer told reporters.
Bullimore, 56, was rescused on Thursday after surviving for four days in an air pocket in his upturned yacht, battered by Antarctic seas 2,600 kms (1,600 miles) from Australia.
The Adelaide also rescued French yachtsman Thierry Dubois, a competitor in the same race.
The Australian, a national newspaper, reported that one of Bullimore's frostbitten fingers might have to be amputated. He has already lost part of another in an accident on the yacht.
He was suffering from hypothermia and dehydration and as the crew took him aboard on Thursday he asked for a cup of tea.

As a search continued for another competitor in the French-organised Vendee Globe solo race, missing Canadian Gerry Roufs, Dubois said future events might have to assign a rescue ship to accompany the yachts.
"Perhaps we have to find a solution," he said from the frigate. "It is a problem with 15 or 16 boats and perhaps in future we will have to have a boat travelling with us."
The yachts of both Dubois and Bullimore capsized in heavy weather, and the Frenchman said that would have to be addressed.
"We have to work with designers about this problem," he said.
Race organisers have lost contact with Canadian Roufs, who is in an even more remote part of the ocean between New Zealand and South America with only a merchant ship searching for him.

A Royal Australian Air Force Orion maritime aircraft saved another race competitor, Frenchman Raphael Dinelli, on December 27 when it found him and dropped a life raft a few minutes before his overturned yacht sank.
The French government, whose 1995 nuclear bomb tests generated great hostility among Pacific nations, thanked Australia for the rescue.

"The French people will not forget the dedication and competence of the Australian Defence Forces that have participated in the rescue of the Vendee Globe Challenge seamen in danger of being lost," French Prime Minister Alain Juppe wrote to his Australian counterpart, John Howard.
"The solidarity Australia has once more shown towards these seamen in distress arouses admiration and gratitude," he said.

Bullimore's against-the-odds survival story is now expected to attract commercial interest. Australian media quoted promotions experts as estimating Bullimore could expect to make A$2 million (US$1.6 million) from his rescue, the closest ever to Antarctica.
His A$1.08 million boat was not insured, The Sydney Morning Herald reported.
Dubois told France 2 television by radio he had been certain of dying but clung to life because he had not seen enough of it.
"I really tried to hang in there," he said. "I am only 29 and I felt it was a pity to call it a day without having seen much of life."

An Orion found Dubois on Monday on his overturned yacht. As another Orion found Bullimore's boat -- with Bullimore inside, as it turned out -- the Royal Australian Navy dispatched the frigate at best speed to rescue the pair, who were well beyond usual merchant shipping lanes.
Orion aircraft watched over the two boats for three days until the ship picked up Dubois early on Thursday and then steamed on to Bullimore's yacht to discover him alive inside.
